**Vignette: Aroha, Age 20**

Aroha grew up on the outskirts of Auckland, the second youngest in a large Māori family where the doors were always unlocked and neighbors moved in and out of each other's homes like the tide. She had been proud of herself for landing a junior auditor position at a mid-sized accounting firm straight out of polytechnic — proud of the early mornings, the spreadsheets, the sense that her life was finally taking a shape she had chosen for herself. That version of her life ended about eight months ago, when she realized that the man she had briefly dated — just four weeks, nothing serious — had not accepted that it was over.

It started with messages. Then her friends began mentioning that he had been asking about her. Then she noticed his car parked outside her apartment building two mornings in a row, and then three. By the time she found a photograph of herself — taken from a distance, without her knowledge — slipped under her door, something inside her had reorganized itself around fear. She went to the police. They documented everything, spoke to him, and for a short while it seemed to stop. Then it started again, quieter, more careful. He began appearing at the edges of her life: the same supermarket aisle, the same bus stop, always just plausibly coincidental. She stopped being able to trust coincidence at all.

Now, eight months later, Aroha sits in sessions with her hands folded tightly in her lap, her eyes tracking the door at intervals she seems unaware of. She describes sleeping in fragments — two hours, then awake, then an hour, then awake again — because the moment her vigilance relaxes, her body pulls her back to the surface. She has moved apartments twice. She has changed her route to work so many times that she now adds forty minutes to her commute, and she has memorized which stairwells in her office building have windows facing the street.

Her work as an auditor, which once felt like a refuge of logic and order, has become a source of its own particular anguish. She is good at her job — meticulous, detail-oriented — but the concentration required has become almost unbearable. She will be midway through reconciling a ledger when a door opens behind her and her heart seizes, her vision narrowing to a single point. She has started requesting desks that face the entrance. She has called in sick on days when she cannot make herself leave her apartment, then spent those days at the window, watching the street below, unable to explain to herself what she is looking for.

She tells her therapist that she does not feel like herself anymore. The person she was — someone who walked home alone without thinking about it, who left her curtains open, who laughed easily — feels like someone she read about once. She replays specific moments obsessively: the photograph under the door, the afternoon she turned around on a busy street and saw him standing thirty meters away, watching her. She wonders what she missed, what she should have done differently, whether something about her invited it. She knows, in the part of her mind that can still reason, that this is not true. But knowing and feeling are not the same thing anymore.

She has pulled back from her family, partly because she does not want to frighten them and partly because she cannot bear the way they look at her — with a helplessness that mirrors her own. Her younger sister has stopped asking why Aroha never comes home on weekends. Aroha tells herself this is easier for everyone.

What she wants, she says quietly, is to walk to the bus stop in the morning without scanning every face. She wants to sit at her desk and think about numbers. She wants to stop waiting for something to happen. She is twenty years old, and she is exhausted in a way she does not have words for yet.
